lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Tiresias — whether you're still blind down here, I honestly can't tell. We all have the same eyes now: empty sockets, no content. You couldn't pick out Phineas from Lynceus at this point. What I do know, from the poets, is that you were a prophet, and that you alone managed to be both a man and a woman. So — in the name of the gods — tell me: which did you find more enjoyable? Life as a man, or was the woman's version better?
lines.note: Menippus opens with a flat observational joke about undead eyes, then pivots to the actual question with studied casualness.

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: The woman's, by a considerable margin, Menippus. Far less bother. Women rule their husbands, and nobody makes them fight wars or stand on the battlements or argue themselves hoarse in the assembly or get cross-examined in court.
lines.note: Tiresias answers with genuine conviction, not embarrassment. The comedy is that he's thought about this.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: You clearly haven't read Euripides' Medea, Tiresias. She has quite a lot to say about the wretchedness of being a woman — the suffering, the unbearable labour of childbirth. [pause] Speaking of which — since Medea's iambics have jogged my memory — did you ever actually give birth, during your time as a woman? Or did you remain barren throughout?
lines.note: The Medea detour is feigned erudition; the real question has been building from the start.

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: What is this, Menippus? Why are you asking me that?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Nothing complicated. Just answer, if it's not too much trouble.

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: I was not barren. But I never — actually gave birth.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Good, that's useful. Though while we're at it — I'd also like to know whether you had a womb.
lines.note: Delivered as a perfectly reasonable follow-up.

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.note: He can hear where this is going and doesn't like it.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: And did the womb disappear gradually — the female parts sealed over, the breasts retracted, the male anatomy growing back in, the beard eventually emerging — or did the change happen all at once, woman to man on the spot?
lines.note: Clinical, methodical, entirely po-faced. The anatomical inventory is the joke.

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: I don't see what you're after with these questions. [pause] Though I can tell you think it didn't happen at all.
lines.note: Tiresias is starting to get irritated.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Oh, so one shouldn't disbelieve these things? One should just accept them — like a simpleton who doesn't stop to ask whether they're actually possible?
lines.note: Menippus states the obvious with perfect courtesy.

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: So you don't believe any of the others either? When you hear that certain women became birds, or trees, or animals — Philomela, Daphne, Lycaon's daughter — you disbelieve those too?
lines.note: Tiresias deploys the appeal to mythological precedent. It doesn't help him.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: If I run into any of them, I'll ask what they have to say. But you — my fine fellow — back when you were a woman: were you already prophesying then, the same as later? Or did you learn to be both a man and a prophet at the same time?
lines.note: Menippus neatly sidesteps the mythological debate and advances the anatomical one.

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: You see? You're ignorant of my entire history. I settled a quarrel between the gods — Hera blinded me for it, and Zeus compensated me with the gift of prophecy.
lines.note: Tiresias pivots to his official biography with the air of someone changing the subject.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Still going with the stories, Tiresias? [pause] But then, that's what prophets do. You people have never said a straight word in your lives.
lines.note: Flat. No heat. The devastation is entirely in the delivery.
